explanations.answer: Arise and come to his aid
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says, “Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid.” Notice who does the moving. David isn't marching out with a sword. He's asking the LORD to get up and come.

Not quite, friend. David never asks to be turned into a warrior. He asks the LORD to take up the shield and buckler and come to his aid. The gear is in the LORD's hands, and I think that says a lot about where David is looking.

Close to a nice thought, but that's not what's on the page. In verse 4, David asks that those who seek his life be disgraced and put to shame. What he asks in verse 2 is for the LORD to arise and come to his aid. This is a psalm where David says his hard stuff out loud.

You got it, baker. David asks the LORD to say to his soul: “I am your salvation.” Spears are nice, but David wants to hear that one sentence. I think a word like that would settle a worried heart faster than any weapon.

explanations.answer: That the fight is almost over
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but David doesn't ask to hear that. He never says how long the fight will last. What he asks the LORD to say to his soul is: “I am your salvation.”

Not this one, friend. David does ask for his pursuers to be driven back, but that's a different request. The words he wants spoken to his soul are: “I am your salvation.” He's asking for the LORD Himself, not just a quiet street.

That's right, baker. David says, “May they be like chaff in the wind, as the angel of the LORD drives them away.” Chaff is the light stuff that blows right off, so it doesn't stand a chance. Nobody argues with wind like that.

Nope, no armies in this verse. David says the one driving them away is the angel of the LORD. The enemies are pictured as chaff in the wind, and chaff doesn't need an army to scatter it. It just needs the wind to blow.
Not quite, friend. The men of Judah never come up in this verse. David says it's the angel of the LORD who drives them away. Verse 6 says the same angel is the one pursuing.

Careful here, baker. David says the opposite. Verse 7 says, “For without cause they laid their net for me; without reason they dug a pit for my soul.” Without cause, without reason. That's David's complaint from start to finish.
That's it, baker. David says they laid their net “without cause” and dug the pit “without reason.” He's not saying they had good reason. He says they had none, and that's exactly why he's crying out.

You got it, baker. David asks, “may the net they hid ensnare them; may they fall into the hazard they created.” The trap they set for him is the one he asks to have catch them. I've left a pan of dough where I'd walk into it before, and I know that feeling.

Not this time, friend. Verse 8 says, “may the net they hid ensnare them; may they fall into the hazard they created.” So David does ask for the net to catch them. The trap they made is the one he asks to have fall on them.

That's the word, baker. David says, “Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.” The fight is loud, but the song ends up somewhere glad. When he's rescued, he knows where the joy goes.
Not quite, friend. David isn't picturing himself hiding. Verse 9 says, “Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.” After the rescue, he's out in the open and glad about it.

Sleep sounds nice after a fight like that, I'll give you that. But the verse says, “Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.” Rejoice is the word, and it sounds pretty wide awake to me.

Right, baker. David's bones say, “Who is like You, O LORD, who delivers the afflicted from the aggressor, the poor and needy from the robber?” He's praising the LORD for helping people who can't help themselves. I think David counts himself among them.

Not this time, friend. The shout in verse 10 includes the words “…the poor and needy from the robber?” So David does say the LORD delivers them. His bones are praising the One who rescues people who can't rescue themselves.
That's right, baker. David says, “They repay me evil for good.” He did good, and he got evil back. That's a hard thing to carry, and he says it plainly.
I wish it were true, friend. But David says, “They repay me evil for good.” Kindness is what he gave, not what he got back.
A thank you would've been nice, wouldn't it? But the verse says, “They repay me evil for good.” David says it leaves his soul bereaved.
Careful, baker. David says it the other way around. Verse 13 says, “…but my prayers returned unanswered.” He fasted and prayed for them, and he says the prayers came back unanswered.

That's the one, baker. David says he put on sackcloth and fasted, “but my prayers returned unanswered.” He doesn't hide it. He just says it, and that honesty is part of why this psalm sticks with people.

You got it, baker. David says, “I paced about as for my friend or brother; I was bowed down with grief, like one mourning for his mother.” He grieved the way you grieve for family. That's what makes what comes next hurt so much.
Not quite, friend. David says he paced about “as for my friend or brother.” He grieved the way he would for someone close, and he says it was like mourning for his mother.
That's not how David puts it. He says he paced about “as for my friend or brother,” and he was bowed down like one mourning for his mother. He grieved like someone who loved them.
That's right, baker. David says, “But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me.” He grieved with them, and they gathered against him. Ouch.
I wish that were the story, friend. Verse 15 says, “But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me.” They didn't come to help. They gathered against him.

That would've been sad enough, but it's not what David says. Verse 15 says, “But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me.” They showed up, and they were glad to see him fall.

Yes, baker. David says, “Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me.” He pictures a room full of mockers at a feast, with the teeth grinding. That's a heavy picture, and I think it hurts to read.
Not this time, friend. Verse 16 says, “Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me.” So David does say it. That's how he describes what they did.

explanations.answer: How long will You look on
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David asks, “How long, O Lord, will You look on?” It's an honest question, and he brings it straight to the Lord. He doesn't take it anywhere else.
That question isn't in this psalm, friend. What David asks is, “How long, O Lord, will You look on?” Then he asks the Lord to rescue his soul.
Not quite, baker. David never asks who they are. He asks, “How long, O Lord, will You look on?” Then he asks the Lord to rescue his soul from their ravages.

That's right, baker. David says, “Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people.” He doesn't plan to thank the LORD quietly in a corner. He wants a crowd to hear it.
That's a place from David's life, but it's not in this psalm. In verse 18 he says, “Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly.” He's picturing a big crowd, not a cave.

Mount Carmel isn't mentioned here, friend. David says, “Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people.” He pictures a big gathering where lots of people hear him.

explanations.answer: Those who live quietly in the land
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. David says, “For they do not speak peace, but they devise deceitful schemes against those who live quietly in the land.” The people being schemed against are the quiet ones. Folks just minding their own business.
Not quite, friend. No priests show up in this verse. David says they devise deceitful schemes “against those who live quietly in the land.”

explanations.answer: The elders at the city gate
explanations.explanation: The elders aren't in this verse, baker. David says the deceitful schemes are against “those who live quietly in the land.” That's regular people living their lives.
You got it, baker. Right after the enemies say, “Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!” David says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent.” They saw him fall. David says the LORD saw all of it.
That's not what David says, friend. He doesn't argue with them about what they saw. He says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent.” His eyes go to the LORD.
Nope, David wants the opposite. He says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me.” He wants the LORD near, not looking away.
That's the word, baker. David says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me.” He wants to hear from the LORD, and he wants Him close.
Not quite, friend. David doesn't mention the LORD being angry here. He says, “be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me.”
Harsh isn't the word, baker. Verse 22 says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me.” David asks the LORD not to be silent, and not to be far.
That's right, baker. David says, “Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God.” He isn't pointing to his own record. He's pointing to who the LORD is.
Not quite, friend. David says, “Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God.” He doesn't hold up his own record. He leans on the LORD's.
That's not what David says, baker. Verse 24 says, “Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God.” The one he's counting on is the LORD, and he doesn't point to any law or court.
Careful, baker. David asks for the opposite. Verse 26 says, “may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach.” He asks for shame and reproach, not honor.

That's it, baker. David says, “May those who gloat in my distress be ashamed and confounded; may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach.” He asks for shame and reproach, not honor. Honor isn't what he asks for them.
Right, baker. David says, “May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness.” He's not alone in this psalm. Some people are on his side, and he wants them shouting.
Not this time, friend. Verse 27 says, “May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness.” So David does want that. Joy and gladness are exactly what he asks for.
You got it, baker. David wants them to always say, “Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant’s well-being.” David calls himself the LORD's servant there. The LORD delights in his well-being.
Not quite, friend. Armies aren't what David wants them saying. He wants them to always say, “Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant’s well-being.”
Not this one, baker. The verse doesn't mention burnt offerings. David wants them to always say, “Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant’s well-being.”

That's right, baker. David says, “Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long.” After a psalm that starts in the middle of a fight, it ends with praise. I'd say that's a good way to finish.
Not quite, friend. David doesn't put an end date on it. He says his tongue will proclaim the LORD's righteousness and praises “all day long.”
Nope, no calendar in this verse, baker. David says, “Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long.” It's not just for special days.
